claim: Human standing balance relies on self-motion estimates that are used by the nervous system to detect unexpected movements and enable corrective responses and adaptations in control.
source: Human standing balance relies on self-motion estimates that are used by the nervous system to detect unexpected movements and enable corrective responses and adaptations in control.
evidence: This is a general statement about balance control presented in the abstract without specific experimental data or citations in this sentence.

claim: Self-motion estimates must accommodate for inherent delays in sensory and motor pathways.
source: These estimates must accommodate for inherent delays in sensory and motor pathways.
evidence: This is a general principle about sensory-motor systems stated in the abstract.

claim: Imposed delays destabilized standing.
source: Imposed delays destabilized standing, but through training, participants adapted and re-learned to balance with the delays.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations reported in the abstract and detailed in the results sections.

claim: Through training, participants adapted and re-learned to balance with the delays.
source: Imposed delays destabilized standing, but through training, participants adapted and re-learned to balance with the delays.
evidence: This claim is supported by training data showing improvement over 5 days of practice.

claim: Before training, imposed delays attenuated vestibular contributions to balance.
source: Before training, imposed delays attenuated vestibular contributions to balance and triggered perceptions of unexpected standing motion, suggesting increased uncertainty in the internal self-motion estimates.
evidence: This is supported by vestibular testing data showing reduced EVS-EMG responses with imposed delays.

claim: Before training, imposed delays triggered perceptions of unexpected standing motion.
source: Before training, imposed delays attenuated vestibular contributions to balance and triggered perceptions of unexpected standing motion, suggesting increased uncertainty in the internal self-motion estimates.
evidence: This is supported by perceptual testing data showing increased detection of unexpected motion with delays.

claim: Imposed delays suggest increased uncertainty in the internal self-motion estimates.
source: Before training, imposed delays attenuated vestibular contributions to balance and triggered perceptions of unexpected standing motion, suggesting increased uncertainty in the internal self-motion estimates.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the vestibular and perceptual data.

claim: After training, vestibular contributions partially returned to baseline levels.
source: After training, vestibular contributions partially returned to baseline levels and larger delays were needed to evoke perceptions of unexpected standing motion.
evidence: This is supported by post-training vestibular testing showing increased EVS-EMG responses compared to pre-training.

claim: After training, larger delays were needed to evoke perceptions of unexpected standing motion.
source: After training, vestibular contributions partially returned to baseline levels and larger delays were needed to evoke perceptions of unexpected standing motion.
evidence: This is supported by rightward shifts in psychometric functions after training.

claim: Through learning, the nervous system accommodates balance sensorimotor delays by causally linking whole-body sensory feedback (initially interpreted as imposed motion) to self-generated balance motor commands.
source: Through learning, the nervous system accommodates balance sensorimotor delays by causally linking whole-body sensory feedback (initially interpreted as imposed motion) to self-generated balance motor commands.
evidence: This is the main conclusion drawn from the combined vestibular and perceptual data.

claim: Errors associated with self-generated movement increase with larger feedback delays.
source: As such, errors associated with self-generated movement increase with larger feedback delays (Gifford and Lyman, 1967; Miall et al., 1985; Smith et al., 1960).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Through repeated exposure to an imposed delay, the brain can learn to expect the delayed feedback associated with self-motion, leading to improvements in movement control with delays up to 430 ms.
source: Through repeated exposure to an imposed delay, the brain can learn to expect the delayed feedback associated with self-motion, leading to improvements in movement control with delays up to 430 ms (Cunningham et al., 2001; Miall and Jackson, 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies on upper-limb adaptation.

claim: When balancing upright, sensory feedback associated with lower-limb motor commands is delayed by up to ~100–160 ms.
source: When balancing upright, sensory feedback associated with lower-limb motor commands is delayed by up to ~100–160 ms (Forbes et al., 2018; Kuo, 2005; van der Kooij et al., 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature on balance control delays.

claim: Computational feedback models of upright standing predict that balance controllers cannot adjust their sensorimotor gains and stabilize balance in the anteroposterior direction with imposed delays larger than ~300–340 ms.
source: As a consequence of these relatively long delays, computational feedback models of upright standing predict that balance controllers cannot adjust their sensorimotor gains and stabilize balance in the anteroposterior (AP) direction with imposed delays larger than ~300–340 ms (Milton and Insperger, 2019; van der Kooij and Peterka, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to computational modeling studies.

claim: Imposed delays inserted within the balance control task are expected to increase postural oscillations and, past a critical delay, lead to falls.
source: Imposed delays inserted within the balance control task are expected to increase postural oscillations and, past a critical delay, lead to falls (Bingham et al., 2011; Milton and Insperger, 2019; van der Kooij and Peterka, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to modeling and experimental studies.

claim: Participants exposed to novel vestibular feedback of balance motion initially exhibit increased postural oscillations but decreased muscle responses to a vestibular error signal.
source: For example, participants exposed to novel vestibular feedback of balance motion initially exhibit increased postural oscillations but decreased muscle responses to a vestibular error signal (Héroux et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: With practice, participants improve their balance and vestibular-evoked muscle responses return to baseline amplitudes, suggesting that the brain updated its vestibular estimates of self-motion.
source: With practice, participants improve their balance and vestibular-evoked muscle responses return to baseline amplitudes, suggesting that the brain updated its vestibular estimates of self-motion.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from cited previous work (Héroux et al., 2015).

claim: Imposed sensorimotor delays during self-generated movements evoke a sensation interpreted to arise from external causes rather than oneself.
source: Imposed sensorimotor delays during self-generated movements evoke a sensation interpreted to arise from external causes rather than oneself (Blakemore et al., 1999; Farrer et al., 2008; Wen, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature on agency and perception.

claim: Repeated exposures to delayed self-generated touch can re-align the perceived timing of the contact with the imposed delay.
source: Repeated exposures to delayed self-generated touch can re-align the perceived timing of the contact with the imposed delay (Kilteni et al., 2019; Stetson et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies on temporal recalibration.

claim: Whole-body sway variability increased with larger imposed delays.
source: Generally, whole-body sway variability increased with larger imposed delays and participants repeatedly fell into virtual limits of the balance simulation (i.e., 6° anterior and 3° posterior) for added delays larger than ~200–300 ms.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from Experiment 1.

claim: Participants repeatedly fell into virtual limits of the balance simulation for added delays larger than ~200–300 ms.
source: Generally, whole-body sway variability increased with larger imposed delays and participants repeatedly fell into virtual limits of the balance simulation (i.e., 6° anterior and 3° posterior) for added delays larger than ~200–300 ms.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from Experiment 1.

claim: Initially, participants exhibited increased postural oscillations while the vestibular contributions to balance decreased and their perception of unexpected balance motion increased.
source: Initially, participants exhibited increased postural oscillations while the vestibular contributions to balance decreased and their perception of unexpected balance motion increased.
evidence: This is supported by pre-training data from Experiment 2.

claim: After training, participants' balance behavior improved, their vestibular-evoked responses increased, and larger imposed delays were needed to elicit perceptions of unexpected balance motion.
source: After training, participants' balance behavior improved, their vestibular-evoked responses increased, and larger imposed delays were needed to elicit perceptions of unexpected balance motion.
evidence: This is supported by post-training data from Experiment 2.

claim: Within a few seconds of transitioning to a 200 ms delay, whole-body sway variability increased, vestibular responses attenuated (~70–90% decline) and participants perceived unexpected balancing motion.
source: Within a few seconds of transitioning to a 200 ms delay, whole-body sway variability increased, vestibular responses attenuated (~70–90% decline) and participants perceived unexpected balancing motion.
evidence: This is supported by data from Experiment 3.

claim: The nervous system can learn to maintain standing balance with imposed delays by associating delayed whole-body motion with self-generated balancing motor commands.
source: Collectively, our findings demonstrate how novel sensorimotor delays disrupt standing balance and suggest that the nervous system can learn to maintain standing balance with imposed delays by associating delayed whole-body motion with self-generated balancing motor commands.
evidence: This is the main conclusion inferred from all three experiments.

claim: All participants maintained standing balance with small postural oscillations around their preferred upright posture at the 20 ms delay (baseline condition).
source: While balancing on the robotic simulator at the 20 ms delay (baseline condition), all participants maintained standing balance with small postural oscillations around their preferred upright posture (sway velocity variance: 0.07 ± 0.07 [°/s]2 [mean ± standard deviation]).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from Experiment 1.

claim: Sway velocity variance at the 20 ms condition was 0.07 ± 0.07 [°/s]2.
source: While balancing on the robotic simulator at the 20 ms delay (baseline condition), all participants maintained standing balance with small postural oscillations around their preferred upright posture (sway velocity variance: 0.07 ± 0.07 [°/s]2 [mean ± standard deviation]).
evidence: This is a direct measurement from Experiment 1.

claim: No participant exceeded the virtual balance limits at the 20 ms condition.
source: No participant exceeded these virtual balance limits at the 20 ms condition (only one participant reached the limit during the 100 ms condition) whereas every participant exceeded the virtual limits at least once within the 60 s balance period when delays were ≥200 ms.
evidence: This is an observation from Experiment 1 data.

claim: Only one participant reached the limit during the 100 ms condition.
source: No participant exceeded these virtual balance limits at the 20 ms condition (only one participant reached the limit during the 100 ms condition) whereas every participant exceeded the virtual limits at least once within the 60 s balance period when delays were ≥200 ms.
evidence: This is an observation from Experiment 1 data.

claim: Every participant exceeded the virtual limits at least once within the 60 s balance period when delays were ≥200 ms.
source: No participant exceeded these virtual balance limits at the 20 ms condition (only one participant reached the limit during the 100 ms condition) whereas every participant exceeded the virtual limits at least once within the 60 s balance period when delays were ≥200 ms.
evidence: This is an observation from Experiment 1 data.

claim: There was a main effect of delay on sway velocity variance (p<0.001).
source: There was a main effect of delay on sway velocity variance (extracted over 2 s windows of continuous balance; Materials and methods), such that sway velocity variance was smallest for the 20 ms condition (0.07 ± 0.07 [°/s]2) and increased with the magnitude of the imposed delay and reached a maximum at 400 ms (21.08 ± 15.41 [°/s]2; p<0.001; Table 1 and Figure 2B).
evidence: This is a statistical result from Experiment 1.

claim: Sway velocity variance reached a maximum at 400 ms (21.08 ± 15.41 [°/s]2).
source: There was a main effect of delay on sway velocity variance (extracted over 2 s windows of continuous balance; Materials and methods), such that sway velocity variance was smallest for the 20 ms condition (0.07 ± 0.07 [°/s]2) and increased with the magnitude of the imposed delay and reached a maximum at 400 ms (21.08 ± 15.41 [°/s]2; p<0.001; Table 1 and Figure 2B).
evidence: This is a measurement from Experiment 1.

claim: There was a main effect of delay on the percent time within the balance limits (p<0.001).
source: We also quantified the percent time participants balanced within the virtual limits. There was a main effect of delay on the percent time within the balance limits (p<0.001; Table 1 and Figure 2B), which decreased from 100% ± 0% during the 20 ms condition to 54% ± 9% during the 500 ms condition.
evidence: This is a statistical result from Experiment 1.

claim: Percent time within balance limits decreased from 100% ± 0% during the 20 ms condition to 54% ± 9% during the 500 ms condition.
source: We also quantified the percent time participants balanced within the virtual limits. There was a main effect of delay on the percent time within the balance limits (p<0.001; Table 1 and Figure 2B), which decreased from 100% ± 0% during the 20 ms condition to 54% ± 9% during the 500 ms condition.
evidence: This is a measurement from Experiment 1.

claim: Participants exhibited greater sway velocity variance compared to the 20 ms condition when imposed delays were ≥200 ms (all p-values <0.05).
source: Decomposition of the main effects revealed that participants exhibited greater sway velocity variance and lower percentage of trial duration within the virtual limits compared to the 20 ms condition when imposed delays were ≥200 ms (all p-values <0.05).
evidence: This is a statistical result from Experiment 1.

claim: Participants exhibited lower percentage of trial duration within the virtual limits compared to the 20 ms condition when imposed delays were ≥200 ms (all p-values <0.05).
source: Decomposition of the main effects revealed that participants exhibited greater sway velocity variance and lower percentage of trial duration within the virtual limits compared to the 20 ms condition when imposed delays were ≥200 ms (all p-values <0.05).
evidence: This is a statistical result from Experiment 1.

claim: Within the first minute of training with the 400 ms delay, no participant could remain upright.
source: Within the first minute of training with the 400 ms delay, no participant could remain upright: on average, they reached the forward or backward virtual balancing limits 18 ± 5 times (see representative participant in Figure 3A) and could only remain within the balancing limits for 64% ± 9 % of the time (or 38.5 s).
evidence: This is an observation from Experiment 2 training data.

claim: On average, participants reached the forward or backward virtual balancing limits 18 ± 5 times in the first minute of training.
source: Within the first minute of training with the 400 ms delay, no participant could remain upright: on average, they reached the forward or backward virtual balancing limits 18 ± 5 times (see representative participant in Figure 3A) and could only remain within the balancing limits for 64% ± 9 % of the time (or 38.5 s).
evidence: This is a measurement from Experiment 2 training data.

claim: Participants could only remain within the balancing limits for 64% ± 9 % of the time (or 38.5 s) in the first minute of training.
source: Within the first minute of training with the 400 ms delay, no participant could remain upright: on average, they reached the forward or backward virtual balancing limits 18 ± 5 times (see representative participant in Figure 3A) and could only remain within the balancing limits for 64% ± 9 % of the time (or 38.5 s).
evidence: This is a measurement from Experiment 2 training data.

claim: Unstable balancing behavior in the first minute was characterized by large whole-body sway velocity variance (12.62 ± 9.03 [°/s]2).
source: This unstable balancing behavior was characterized by large whole-body sway velocity variance (12.62 ± 9.03 [°/s]2).
evidence: This is a measurement from Experiment 2 training data.

claim: During training, participants progressively reduced the variance of their sway velocity and increased the percentage of time they balanced within the virtual limits.
source: During training, participants progressively reduced the variance of their sway velocity and increased the percentage of time they balanced within the virtual limits.
evidence: This is an observation from Experiment 2 training data.

claim: By the end of training (100 min), participants exhibited an ~80% decrease in sway velocity variance and a 51% increase in percent time within the virtual limits.
source: By the end of training (100 min), participants exhibited an ~80% decrease in sway velocity variance and a 51% increase in percent time within the virtual limits.
evidence: This is a measurement from Experiment 2 training data.

claim: The time constant for the decrease in sway velocity variance was 27.9 min.
source: The time constant for the decrease in sway velocity variance (i.e., 63.2% attenuation) was 27.9 min (corresponding to a value of 6.44 [°/s]2), and the time constant for the increase in percent time within limits (i.e., 63.2% increase) was 32.5 min (corresponding to a value of 85% within the balance limits).
evidence: This is derived from exponential fitting of Experiment 2 training data.

claim: The time constant for the increase in percent time within limits was 32.5 min.
source: The time constant for the decrease in sway velocity variance (i.e., 63.2% attenuation) was 27.9 min (corresponding to a value of 6.44 [°/s]2), and the time constant for the increase in percent time within limits (i.e., 63.2% increase) was 32.5 min (corresponding to a value of 85% within the balance limits).
evidence: This is derived from exponential fitting of Experiment 2 training data.

claim: By the last 60 s of training, participants could balance the robot within the simulation limits on average for 97% ± 3% of the time.
source: By the last 60 s of training, participants could balance the robot within the simulation limits on average for 97% ± 3% of the time (or 59.2 s), with four participants capable of balancing for the final 60 s interval without reaching a limit.
evidence: This is a measurement from Experiment 2 training data.

claim: Four participants were capable of balancing for the final 60 s interval without reaching a limit.
source: By the last 60 s of training, participants could balance the robot within the simulation limits on average for 97% ± 3% of the time (or 59.2 s), with four participants capable of balancing for the final 60 s interval without reaching a limit.
evidence: This is an observation from Experiment 2 training data.

claim: The smallest sway velocity variance observed with a 400 ms imposed delay remained ~38× greater than the baseline condition.
source: However, the smallest sway velocity variance observed with a 400 ms imposed delay remained ~38× greater than the baseline condition (400 ms at 93rd min vs. 20 ms variance: 1.91 ± 1.12 [°/s]2 vs. 0.05 ± 0.05 [°/s]2; t(15) = 6.74: p<0.001).
evidence: This is a statistical comparison from Experiment 2 training data.

claim: Sway velocity variance in the first minute of retention testing was ~60.8% lower than the sway velocity variance from the first minute of training.
source: Sway velocity variance in the first minute of retention testing was ~60.8% lower than the sway velocity variance from the first minute of training (4.95 ± 2.32 [°/s]2 vs. 12.62 ± 9.03 [°/s]2; independent samples t-test: t(26) = –2.86, p<0.01).
evidence: This is a statistical comparison from Experiment 2 retention data.

claim: Sway velocity variance at the first minute of retention testing remained greater than the last minute of training.
source: Sway velocity variance at the first minute of retention testing, however, remained greater than the last minute of training (4.95 ± 2.32 [°/s]2 vs. 2.55 ± 1.76 [°/s]2; independent samples t-test: t(26) = 3.11, p<0.01).
evidence: This is a statistical comparison from Experiment 2 retention data.

claim: The first minute of retention was associated with a greater percentage of time within the balancing limits compared to the first minute of training (88% ± 9% vs. 64% ± 9%).
source: Similarly, the first minute of retention was associated with a greater percentage of time within the balancing limits compared to the first minute of training (88% ± 9% vs. 64% ± 9%; independent samples t-test: t(26) = 6.67, p<0.001), but less than the last minute of training (88% ± 9% vs. 97% ± 3%; independent samples t-test: t(26) = –3.68, p<0.01).
evidence: This is a statistical comparison from Experiment 2 retention data.

claim: The first minute of retention was associated with less percentage of time within the balancing limits than the last minute of training (88% ± 9% vs. 97% ± 3%).
source: Similarly, the first minute of retention was associated with a greater percentage of time within the balancing limits compared to the first minute of training (88% ± 9% vs. 64% ± 9%; independent samples t-test: t(26) = 6.67, p<0.001), but less than the last minute of training (88% ± 9% vs. 97% ± 3%; independent samples t-test: t(26) = –3.68, p<0.01).
evidence: This is a statistical comparison from Experiment 2 retention data.

claim: While standing with an imposed 400 ms delay is initially difficult (if not impossible), participants learn to balance with the delay with sufficient training (i.e., >30 min) and this ability is partially retained 3 months later.
source: Overall, these results indicate that while standing with an imposed 400 ms delay is initially difficult (if not impossible), participants learn to balance with the delay with sufficient training (i.e., >30 min) and this ability is partially retained 3 months later.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from Experiment 2 training and retention data.

claim: Vestibular-evoked muscle responses are known to attenuate when actual sensory feedback does not align with expected estimates from balancing motor commands.
source: Vestibular-evoked muscle responses are known to attenuate when actual sensory feedback does not align with expected estimates from balancing motor commands (Héroux et al., 2015; Luu et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Participants exhibited the largest vestibular-evoked muscle responses (coherence, gain, and cross-covariance) for the 20 and 100 ms delay conditions.
source: Participants exhibited the largest vestibular-evoked muscle responses (coherence, gain,and cross-covariance) for the 20 and 100 ms delay conditions, where significant coherence was observed at frequencies between 0 and 25 Hz and cross-covariance responses were characterized by short (~60 ms) and medium (~100 ms) latency peaks exceeding the 95% confidence interval (see Figure 4A).
evidence: This is an observation from Experiment 2 vestibular testing data.

claim: Prior to learning, pooled coherence and gain decreased with imposed delays ≥ 200 ms.
source: Prior to learning, pooled coherence and gain decreased with imposed delays ≥ 200 ms, and coherence fell below the significance threshold at most frequencies for delays ≥ 300 ms.
evidence: This is an observation from Experiment 2 vestibular testing data.

claim: Coherence fell below the significance threshold at most frequencies for delays ≥ 300 ms prior to learning.
source: Prior to learning, pooled coherence and gain decreased with imposed delays ≥ 200 ms, and coherence fell below the significance threshold at most frequencies for delays ≥ 300 ms.
evidence: This is an observation from Experiment 2 vestibular testing data.

claim: Cross-covariance amplitudes decreased with increasing delay (≥200 ms) prior to learning.
source: Similarly, cross-covariance amplitudes decreased with increasing delay (≥200 ms), with only five out of eight participants showing significant biphasic muscle responses (cross-covariance) for the 400 ms delay condition (and six out of eight participants at 500 ms).
evidence: This is an observation from Experiment 2 vestibular testing data.

claim: Only five out of eight participants showed significant biphasic muscle responses for the 400 ms delay condition prior to learning.
source: Similarly, cross-covariance amplitudes decreased with increasing delay (≥200 ms), with only five out of eight participants showing significant biphasic muscle responses (cross-covariance) for the 400 ms delay condition (and six out of eight participants at 500 ms).
evidence: This is an observation from Experiment 2 vestibular testing data.

claim: Across training conditions (pre, post, retention), increasing the delay reduced the cross-covariance peak-to-peak amplitudes (main effect of delay, p<0.001).
source: Across training conditions (pre, post, retention), increasing the delay reduced the cross-covariance peak-to-peak amplitudes (main effect of delay, p<0.001; Figure 4A and B, Table 1).
evidence: This is a statistical result from Experiment 2 vestibular testing.

claim: Following training, pooled vestibular-evoked muscle responses (coherence, gain, cross-covariance) partially recovered in both the post-learning and retention phases.
source: Following training, pooled vestibular-evoked muscle responses (coherence, gain, cross-covariance) partially recovered in both the post-learning and retention phases.
evidence: This is an observation from Experiment 2 vestibular testing data.

claim: Every participant exhibited biphasic muscle responses that exceeded significance thresholds for every delay after training.
source: Every participant exhibited biphasic muscle responses that exceeded significance thresholds for every delay after training.
evidence: This is an observation from Experiment 2 vestibular testing data.

claim: A significant interaction between delay and learning was observed for the cross-covariance (p<0.001).
source: A significant interaction between delay and learning was observed for the cross-covariance (p<0.001, Table 1), suggesting that the recovery of vestibular responses was dependent on the delay magnitude.
evidence: This is a statistical result from Experiment 2 vestibular testing.

claim: Cross-covariance response amplitudes were larger during post-learning relative to pre-learning for delays ≥ 200 ms (all p-values <0.05).
source: Planned comparisons (Wilcoxon sign-rank test, Bonferroni corrected) revealed that cross-covariance response amplitudes were larger during post-learning relative to pre-learning for delays ≥ 200 ms (all p-values <0.05) and were larger during retention relative to pre-learning for 300 and 400 ms (p<0.05).
evidence: This is a statistical result from Experiment 2 vestibular testing.

claim: Cross-covariance response amplitudes were larger during retention relative to pre-learning for 300 and 400 ms (p<0.05).
source: Planned comparisons (Wilcoxon sign-rank test, Bonferroni corrected) revealed that cross-covariance response amplitudes were larger during post-learning relative to pre-learning for delays ≥ 200 ms (all p-values <0.05) and were larger during retention relative to pre-learning for 300 and 400 ms (p<0.05).
evidence: This is a statistical result from Experiment 2 vestibular testing.

claim: Sway velocity variance generally increased with increasing delays (p<0.001) in vestibular testing.
source: Similar to Experiment 1, sway velocity variance generally increased with increasing delays (Figure 4C, Table 1, Table 2; p<0.001), while learning decreased sway velocity variance at almost all imposed delays (Figure 4C, Table 1; p<0.001), resulting in a significant delay × learning interaction (Figure 4C, Table 1; p<0.001).
evidence: This is a statistical result from Experiment 2 vestibular testing.

claim: Learning decreased sway velocity variance at almost all imposed delays (p<0.001) in vestibular testing.
source: Similar to Experiment 1, sway velocity variance generally increased with increasing delays (Figure 4C, Table 1, Table 2; p<0.001), while learning decreased sway velocity variance at almost all imposed delays (Figure 4C, Table 1; p<0.001), resulting in a significant delay × learning interaction (Figure 4C, Table 1; p<0.001).
evidence: This is a statistical result from Experiment 2 vestibular testing.

claim: There was a significant delay × learning interaction for sway velocity variance (p<0.001) in vestibular testing.
source: Similar to Experiment 1, sway velocity variance generally increased with increasing delays (Figure 4C, Table 1, Table 2; p<0.001), while learning decreased sway velocity variance at almost all imposed delays (Figure 4C, Table 1; p<0.001), resulting in a significant delay × learning interaction (Figure 4C, Table 1; p<0.001).
evidence: This is a statistical result from Experiment 2 vestibular testing.

claim: Sway velocity variance decreased during post-learning relative to pre-learning for delays between 20 and 400 ms (all p-values <0.05).
source: Planned comparisons (paired t-tests, Bonferroni corrected) revealed that sway velocity variance decreased during post-learning relative to pre-learning for delays between 20 and 400 ms (all p-values <0.05) and decreased during retention relative to pre-learning for delays between 100 and 400 ms (all p-values <0.05).
evidence: This is a statistical result from Experiment 2 vestibular testing.

claim: Sway velocity variance decreased during retention relative to pre-learning for delays between 100 and 400 ms (all p-values <0.05).
source: Planned comparisons (paired t-tests, Bonferroni corrected) revealed that sway velocity variance decreased during post-learning relative to pre-learning for delays between 20 and 400 ms (all p-values <0.05) and decreased during retention relative to pre-learning for delays between 100 and 400 ms (all p-values <0.05).
evidence: This is a statistical result from Experiment 2 vestibular testing.

claim: Training was only performed with the 400 ms delay.
source: Because training was only performed with the 400 ms delay, these training-related changes in vestibular responses (cross-covariance) and sway behavior across delays indicate that learning generalized to different sensorimotor delays.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design.

claim: Training-related changes in vestibular responses and sway behavior across delays indicate that learning generalized to different sensorimotor delays.
source: Because training was only performed with the 400 ms delay, these training-related changes in vestibular responses (cross-covariance) and sway behavior across delays indicate that learning generalized to different sensorimotor delays.
evidence: This is an inference from the observation that improvements occurred at delays other than the trained 400 ms delay.

claim: Behavioral studies in humans suggest that delayed self-motion is perceived as unexpected (or externally imposed) because it does not align with prior expectations of the intended movement.
source: Behavioral studies in humans suggest that delayed self-motion is perceived as unexpected (or externally imposed) because it does not align with prior expectations of the intended movement (Blakemore et al., 1999; Farrer et al., 2008; Wen, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The probability of perceiving unexpected postural motion increased with delays: from 4% detection for the 50 ms delay up to 100% for the 350 ms delay.
source: Across participants, the probability of perceiving unexpected postural motion increased with delays: from 4% detection for the 50 ms delay up to 100% for the 350 ms delay (Table 3).
evidence: This is an observation from Experiment 2 perceptual testing data.

claim: On average, when unexpected balance motion was correctly detected, participants pressed the button at least ~2 s after the delay was imposed across all delays and learning conditions.
source: On average, when unexpected balance motion was correctly detected, participants pressed the button at least ~2 s after the delay was imposed across all delays and learning conditions (Table 3).
evidence: This is an observation from Experiment 2 perceptual testing data.

claim: After participants completed training with the 400 ms delay, psychometric functions shifted to the right, resulting in increased thresholds for detecting unexpected balance movements (p=0.008).
source: After participants (n = 8) completed training with the 400 ms delay, psychometric functions shifted to the right, resulting in increased thresholds for detecting unexpected balance movements (Figure 5A and B, Table 1; p=0.008, Bonferroni corrected).
evidence: This is a statistical result from Experiment 2 perceptual testing.

claim: Thresholds were larger during post-learning relative to pre-learning (192 ± 40 ms vs. 147 ± 21 ms; p=0.032).
source: Thresholds were larger during post-learning relative to pre-learning (Figure 5B; 192 ± 40 ms vs. 147 ± 21 ms; p=0.032, Bonferroni corrected) and were larger for retention relative to pre-learning (209 ± 82 ms vs. 147 ± 21 ms; p=0.014, Bonferroni corrected).
evidence: This is a statistical result from Experiment 2 perceptual testing.

claim: Thresholds were larger for retention relative to pre-learning (209 ± 82 ms vs. 147 ± 21 ms; p=0.014).
source: Thresholds were larger during post-learning relative to pre-learning (Figure 5B; 192 ± 40 ms vs. 147 ± 21 ms; p=0.032, Bonferroni corrected) and were larger for retention relative to pre-learning (209 ± 82 ms vs. 147 ± 21 ms; p=0.014, Bonferroni corrected).
evidence: This is a statistical result from Experiment 2 perceptual testing.

claim: There were significant main effects of delay (p<0.001) and learning (p<0.001) as well as a delay × learning interaction (p=0.023) for sway velocity variance in perceptual testing.
source: For the whole-body oscillations (sway velocity variance extracted over the 8 s periods when delays were imposed, see Table 1), we again confirmed significant main effects of delay (p<0.001) and learning (p<0.001) as well as a delay × learning interaction (p=0.023).
evidence: This is a statistical result from Experiment 2 perceptual testing.

claim: Sway velocity variance decreased during post-learning relative to pre-learning for delays ranging from 150 to 250 ms (all p-values <0.05) in perceptual testing.
source: Planned comparisons (paired t-tests, Bonferroni corrected) revealed that sway velocity variance decreased during post-learning relative to pre-learning for delays ranging from 150 to 250 ms (all p-values <0.05) and decreased during retention relative to pre-learning for the 150, 200, 300, and 350 delays (all p-values <0.05).
evidence: This is a statistical result from Experiment 2 perceptual testing.

claim: Sway velocity variance decreased during retention relative to pre-learning for the 150, 200, 300, and 350 delays (all p-values <0.05) in perceptual testing.
source: Planned comparisons (paired t-tests, Bonferroni corrected) revealed that sway velocity variance decreased during post-learning relative to pre-learning for delays ranging from 150 to 250 ms (all p-values <0.05) and decreased during retention relative to pre-learning for the 150, 200, 300, and 350 delays (all p-values <0.05).
evidence: This is a statistical result from Experiment 2 perceptual testing.

claim: Out of the 588 total transitions in Experiment 3, 489 were perceived as eliciting unexpected balance motion and used for all analyses.
source: Out of the 588 total transitions, 489 were perceived as eliciting unexpected balance motion and used for all analyses.

claim: Transitions between baseline and delayed balance control increased whole-body sway velocity variance throughout most of the delay period in Experiment 3.
source: Transitions between baseline and delayed balance control increased whole-body sway velocity variance throughout most of the delay period (see Figure 6A).
evidence: This is an observation from Experiment 3 data.

claim: Over the delay period, coherence and gain between EVS and EMG decreased in Experiment 3.
source: Over the same period, coherence and gain between EVS and EMG decreased.
evidence: This is an observation from Experiment 3 data.

claim: The 63.2% attenuation for coherence occurred at 1.5 ± 0.6 s following delay onset in Experiment 3.
source: The 63.2% attenuation (i.e., the time constant) for coherence occurred at 1.5 ± 0.6 s following delay onset while the 95% attenuation (i.e., 3× time constant) occurred at 4.4 ± 2.6 s following delay onset.
evidence: This is derived from exponential fitting of Experiment 3 data.

claim: The 95% attenuation for coherence occurred at 4.4 ± 2.6 s following delay onset in Experiment 3.
source: The 63.2% attenuation (i.e., the time constant) for coherence occurred at 1.5 ± 0.6 s following delay onset while the 95% attenuation (i.e., 3× time constant) occurred at 4.4 ± 2.6 s following delay onset.
evidence: This is derived from exponential fitting of Experiment 3 data.

claim: The 63.2% attenuation from the mean gain estimate occurred at 2.3 s in Experiment 3.
source: For gain, we fit an exponential decay only to the mean gain estimated from the pooled data because for some participants coherence decreased below significance at all frequencies for some periods of the delay exposure (see Figure 6C, left-lower panel). The 63.2% attenuation from this mean gain estimate occurred at 2.3 s while the 95% attenuation occurred at 6.8 s.
evidence: This is derived from exponential fitting of Experiment 3 pooled data.

claim: The 95% attenuation from the mean gain estimate occurred at 6.8 s in Experiment 3.
source: For gain, we fit an exponential decay only to the mean gain estimated from the pooled data because for some participants coherence decreased below significance at all frequencies for some periods of the delay exposure (see Figure 6C, left-lower panel). The 63.2% attenuation from this mean gain estimate occurred at 2.3 s while the 95% attenuation occurred at 6.8 s.
evidence: This is derived from exponential fitting of Experiment 3 pooled data.

claim: The group averaged detection occurred at 3.4 ± 1.8 s after delay onset in Experiment 3.
source: Perceptual detection times occurred over a similar time period, with the group averaged (489 detections) detection occurring at 3.4 ± 1.8 s after delay onset (see magenta line in Figure 6, right panel) and the 95th percentile for detection time occurring at 6.9 ± 0.8 s.
evidence: This is a measurement from Experiment 3 data.

claim: The 95th percentile for detection time occurred at 6.9 ± 0.8 s in Experiment 3.
source: Perceptual detection times occurred over a similar time period, with the group averaged (489 detections) detection occurring at 3.4 ± 1.8 s after delay onset (see magenta line in Figure 6, right panel) and the 95th percentile for detection time occurring at 6.9 ± 0.8 s.
evidence: This is a measurement from Experiment 3 data.

claim: The average time to detect the imposed delay (3.4 ± 1.8 s) corresponded to a 90% ± 7% average reduction in mean coherence in Experiment 3.
source: Comparing the perceptual detection timing with the exponential decrease in coherence estimated from each participant, we found that the average time to detect the imposed delay (3.4 ± 1.8 s) corresponded to a 90% ± 7% average reduction in mean coherence.
evidence: This is a comparison of perceptual and vestibular data from Experiment 3.

claim: The average perceptual time aligned with a 73% reduction in gain in Experiment 3.
source: For the mean gain estimate (from all participants), this average perceptual time aligned with a 73% reduction in gain.
evidence: This is a comparison of perceptual and vestibular data from Experiment 3.

claim: The peak velocity variance leading up to a perceptual detection resulted in an average peak velocity variance of 8.42 ± 8.62 [°/s]2 in Experiment 3.
source: The peak velocity variance leading up to a perceptual detection was also extracted for each perceived transition and resulted in an average peak velocity variance of 8.42 ± 8.62 [°/s]2.
evidence: This is a measurement from Experiment 3 data.

claim: The perception of unexpected motion and increased sway variability arising from an imposed delay are accompanied by an ~70–90% attenuation of vestibular contributions to balance.
source: Overall, these results indicate that the perception of unexpected motion and increased sway variability arising from an imposed delay are accompanied by an ~70–90% attenuation of vestibular contributions to balance.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from Experiment 3 data.

claim: When delays were first imposed, the variance of whole-body sway velocity during balance increased with larger delays and all participants exceeded the virtual balance limits when delays were ≥200 ms.
source: When delays were first imposed, the variance of whole-body sway velocity during balance increased with larger delays and all participants exceeded the virtual balance limits (6° anterior, 3° posterior) when delays were ≥200 ms.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from Experiment 1.

claim: Balancing with imposed delays attenuated vestibular-evoked muscle responses and led to perceptions of unexpected movement during standing balance.
source: Balancing with imposed delays also attenuated vestibular-evoked muscle responses and led to perceptions of unexpected movement during standing balance, supporting the interpretation that imposing delays increased uncertainty in the internal estimate of balancing self-motion.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from Experiment 2.

claim: Imposing delays increased uncertainty in the internal estimate of balancing self-motion.
source: Balancing with imposed delays also attenuated vestibular-evoked muscle responses and led to perceptions of unexpected movement during standing balance, supporting the interpretation that imposing delays increased uncertainty in the internal estimate of balancing self-motion.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the vestibular and perceptual findings.

claim: Participants learned to balance with an imposed sensorimotor delay of 400 ms over 5 days (100 min of training), showing decreased sway velocity variance and increased percent time balancing within the virtual limits.
source: Importantly, participants learned to balance with an imposed sensorimotor delay of 400 ms over 5 days (100 min of training), showing decreased sway velocity variance and increased percent time balancing within the virtual limits, partially restored vestibular control of balance, and fewer unexpected movement detections while balancing with the delay.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from Experiment 2 training.

claim: Training led to partially restored vestibular control of balance.
source: Importantly, participants learned to balance with an imposed sensorimotor delay of 400 ms over 5 days (100 min of training), showing decreased sway velocity variance and increased percent time balancing within the virtual limits, partially restored vestibular control of balance, and fewer unexpected movement detections while balancing with the delay.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from Experiment 2 vestibular testing.

claim: Training led to fewer unexpected movement detections while balancing with the delay.
source: Importantly, participants learned to balance with an imposed sensorimotor delay of 400 ms over 5 days (100 min of training), showing decreased sway velocity variance and increased percent time balancing within the virtual limits, partially restored vestibular control of balance, and fewer unexpected movement detections while balancing with the delay.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from Experiment 2 perceptual testing.

claim: Learning effects were generalized across delays despite training to balance only at the 400 ms delay.
source: These effects were generalized across delays despite training to balance only at the 400 ms delay.
evidence: This is an inference from the observation that improvements occurred at multiple delays.

claim: While there may be a critical delay for the balance system, the brain can find a solution to overcome this limitation.
source: Our findings reveal that, while there may be a critical delay for the balance system, the brain can find a solution to overcome this limitation, learning to maintain standing balance with imposed delays by causally linking delayed whole-body sensory feedback that was initially interpreted as imposed motion to self-generated balance motor commands.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the overall findings.

claim: The brain can learn to maintain standing balance with imposed delays by causally linking delayed whole-body sensory feedback that was initially interpreted as imposed motion to self-generated balance motor commands.
source: Our findings reveal that, while there may be a critical delay for the balance system, the brain can find a solution to overcome this limitation, learning to maintain standing balance with imposed delays by causally linking delayed whole-body sensory feedback that was initially interpreted as imposed motion to self-generated balance motor commands.
evidence: This is the main mechanistic conclusion from the study.

claim: The nervous system can learn to control standing balance with a net delay of up to 500–560 ms.
source: Our results, in contrast, clearly demonstrate that participants improved their balance behavior (i.e., reduced sway velocity variance) when given the opportunity to train with a 400 ms delay (~63% by 28–33 min), and that this improvement was retained, at least partially, 3 months later. Therefore, the nervous system can learn to control standing balance (although with more variability) with a net delay of up to 500–560 ms.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the training data showing learning at 400 ms imposed delay plus the inherent ~100-160 ms physiological delay.

claim: Optimal controllers can model the control of human standing.
source: Compared to feedback controllers (i.e., PD and proportional-integral-derivative), which are not optimal in the presence of delays, optimal controllers can model the control of human standing (Kiemel et al., 2002; Kuo, 1995; Kuo, 2005; van der Kooij et al., 1999; van der Kooij et al., 2001) and theoretically stabilize human standing with large (>500 ms) delays (Kuo, 1995).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous modeling studies.

claim: Optimal controllers can theoretically stabilize human standing with large (>500 ms) delays.
source: Compared to feedback controllers (i.e., PD and proportional-integral-derivative), which are not optimal in the presence of delays, optimal controllers can model the control of human standing (Kiemel et al., 2002; Kuo, 1995; Kuo, 2005; van der Kooij et al., 1999; van der Kooij et al., 2001) and theoretically stabilize human standing with large (>500 ms) delays (Kuo, 1995).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a modeling study.

claim: The ability of optimal controllers to stabilize standing rapidly declines with increasing center of mass accelerations.
source: This ability, however, rapidly declines with increasing center of mass accelerations (Kuo, 1995), including those driven by external disturbances (Zhou and Wang, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to modeling studies.

claim: Intermittent corrective balance actions may represent a solution when time delays rule out continuous control.
source: Although feedback and optimal controllers assume that the nervous system linearly and continuously modulates the balancing torques to stand (Fitzpatrick et al., 1996; Masani et al., 2006; van der Kooij and de Vlugt, 2007; Vette et al., 2007), intermittent corrective balance actions (Asai et al., 2009; Bottaro et al., 2005; Gawthrop et al., 2011; Loram et al., 2011; Loram et al., 2005) may represent a solution when time delays rule out continuous control (Gawthrop and Wang, 2006; Arsan et al., 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies on intermittent control.

claim: Intermittent muscle activations are sufficient to stabilize the upright body during a robotic standing balance task similar to the one used in the present study.
source: Intermittent muscle activations are also sufficient to stabilize the upright body during a robotic standing balance task similar to the one used in the present study (Huryn et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: The nervous system may use a combination of controllers during standing.
source: The nervous system may use a combination of the controllers during standing (Elias et al., 2014; Insperger et al., 2015), but our study did not explicitly test for evidence of these different controllers or their ability to stabilize upright stance with large delays.
evidence: This is a speculation based on cited literature, with acknowledgment that the current study did not test this.

claim: The attenuation of vestibular-evoked responses to increased sensorimotor delays could be explained through processes of sensory reweighting.
source: The attenuation of vestibular-evoked responses to increased sensorimotor delays could be explained through processes of sensory reweighting (Cenciarini and Peterka, 2006; Peterka, 2002), where the decreasing reliability in sensory cues when balancing with additional delays decreases feedback gains.
evidence: This is a potential explanation supported by citations to previous work on sensory reweighting.

claim: Feedback control models of standing predict that sensorimotor gains should decrease with increasing sensorimotor delays.
source: Indeed, feedback control models of standing predict that sensorimotor gains should decrease with increasing sensorimotor delays (Bingham et al., 2011; Le Mouel and Brette, 2019; van der Kooij and Peterka, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to modeling studies.

claim: The partial return of vestibular response amplitude and shifted perceptual responses after training indicate the involvement of alternative processes of sensorimotor recalibration.
source: However, our results show the partial return of vestibular response amplitude and shifted perceptual responses after training at a delay of 400 ms, indicating the involvement of alternative processes of sensorimotor recalibration.
evidence: This is an inference from the training data showing recovery of vestibular responses and perceptual shifts.

claim: Both the vestibular and perceptual measures are influenced by whether the brain interprets sensory feedback as self-generated (expected) or externally imposed (unexpected).
source: Both the vestibular and perceptual measures are influenced by whether the brain interprets sensory feedback as self-generated (expected) or externally imposed (unexpected), and their adaptation indicates that the nervous system learned to expect the delayed balancing-related feedback associated with self-generated balancing motor commands.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the vestibular and perceptual findings.

claim: The adaptation of vestibular and perceptual measures indicates that the nervous system learned to expect the delayed balancing-related feedback associated with self-generated balancing motor commands.
source: Both the vestibular and perceptual measures are influenced by whether the brain interprets sensory feedback as self-generated (expected) or externally imposed (unexpected), and their adaptation indicates that the nervous system learned to expect the delayed balancing-related feedback associated with self-generated balancing motor commands.
evidence: This is an inference from the training-related changes in vestibular and perceptual responses.

claim: When first standing with altered vestibular feedback (via a head-coupled EVS), variability in balance behavior increased and the amplitude of vestibular-evoked muscle responses decreased.
source: Similar recalibration of the vestibular control of balance has been observed when humans stand with manipulated vestibular feedback gains (Héroux et al., 2015). When first standing with altered vestibular feedback (via a head-coupled EVS), variability in balance behavior increased and the amplitude of vestibular-evoked muscle responses (probed with an independent EVS signal) decreased.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: After a short (240 s) calibration period with the novel head-coupled vestibular stimulus, postural sway and vestibular responses returned to baseline levels.
source: After a short (240 s) calibration period with the novel head-coupled vestibular stimulus, postural sway and vestibular responses returned to baseline levels (Héroux et al., 2015), suggesting that the brain learned to expect the modified vestibular feedback.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: The recalibration to head-coupled vestibular stimulus could not be explained by sensory reweighting mechanisms since adaptation did not occur when applying matching levels of EVS that were uncoupled from head motion.
source: Notably, this could not be explained by sensory reweighting mechanisms since adaptation did not occur when applying matching levels of EVS that were uncoupled from head motion.
evidence: This is an inference from the cited study (Héroux et al., 2015).

claim: Following repeated exposure to imposed sensorimotor delays, the perceived timing between motor actions and sensory feedback can be shifted according to the magnitude of the delay.
source: Perceptually, there is similar evidence of recalibration to new sensorimotor delays. Following repeated exposure to imposed sensorimotor delays, the perceived timing between motor actions and sensory feedback can be shifted according to the magnitude of the delay (Stetson et al., 2006) and the perceived intensity (i.e., force, tickle sensation) of delayed touch returns to baseline (i.e., no delay) levels (Kilteni et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies on temporal recalibration.

claim: The perceived intensity of delayed touch returns to baseline levels after repeated exposure.
source: Perceptually, there is similar evidence of recalibration to new sensorimotor delays. Following repeated exposure to imposed sensorimotor delays, the perceived timing between motor actions and sensory feedback can be shifted according to the magnitude of the delay (Stetson et al., 2006) and the perceived intensity (i.e., force, tickle sensation) of delayed touch returns to baseline (i.e., no delay) levels (Kilteni et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: These forms of recalibration are possible for the vestibular control of standing balance and the perception of standing balance.
source: Our results suggest that these forms of recalibration are possible for the vestibular control of standing balance and the perception of standing balance.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the current study's findings in the context of previous literature.

claim: We naturally experience changing neural delays during growth and aging.
source: Because we naturally experience changing neural delays during growth and aging (Eyre et al., 1991), it is crucial that the nervous system adapts and recalibrates to unexpected temporal relationships between sensory and motor signals to maintain stable balance control and perception of standing movement.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: It is crucial that the nervous system adapts and recalibrates to unexpected temporal relationships between sensory and motor signals to maintain stable balance control and perception of standing movement.
source: Because we naturally experience changing neural delays during growth and aging (Eyre et al., 1991), it is crucial that the nervous system adapts and recalibrates to unexpected temporal relationships between sensory and motor signals to maintain stable balance control and perception of standing movement.
evidence: This is a general statement about the importance of adaptation based on the study's findings and cited literature.

claim: When faced with a new sensorimotor relationship, deep cerebellar neurons (rostral fastigial nucleus) initially increase their activity to vestibular signals because the motor commands result in unexpected sensory feedback.
source: When faced with a new sensorimotor relationship, deep cerebellar neurons (rostral fastigial nucleus) initially increase their activity to vestibular signals because the motor commands result in unexpected sensory feedback (Brooks et al., 2015; Brooks and Cullen, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to neurophysiological studies.

claim: Learning a new sensorimotor relationship results in a gradual increase in the probability that unexpected feedback arises from desired motor commands, leading to a gradual return of the normal firing patterns of the deep cerebellar neurons.
source: Learning this new sensorimotor relationship results in a gradual increase in the probability that this unexpected feedback arises from desired motor commands, leading to a gradual return of the normal firing patterns of the deep cerebellar neurons (Brooks et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a neurophysiological study.

claim: Neuronal recordings indicate that the nervous system scales responses to sensory inputs based on the relative probability that sensory feedback is caused by motor actions.
source: These neuronal recordings further indicate that the nervous system scales responses (i.e., not a switch-like mechanism) to sensory inputs based on the relative probability that sensory feedback is caused by motor actions.
evidence: This is an inference from cited neurophysiological studies.

claim: Vestibular response amplitudes gradually decreased with the magnitude of the delay, reflecting a mechanism where the nervous system scales responses based on the relative probability that sensory feedback is caused by motor actions.
source: Our vestibular experiment results reflect a similar mechanism – vestibular response amplitudes gradually decreased with the magnitude of the delay – extending this framework to a standing balance control context.
evidence: This is an inference connecting the current study's findings to the neurophysiological framework from cited studies.

claim: Training led to modified vestibular and perceptual responses as well as decreased sway velocity variance that transferred to different imposed delays, indicating a generalized effect of learning.
source: Additionally, training led to modified vestibular and perceptual responses as well as decreased sway velocity variance that transferred to different imposed delays, indicating a generalized effect of learning.
evidence: This is an observation from the training data showing improvements at multiple delays.

claim: The nervous system did not specifically recalibrate sensorimotor cues to the 400 ms delay but estimated the source of the unexpected balance motion and broadly updated its control to accommodate for imposed delays.
source: This suggests that the nervous system did not specifically recalibrate sensorimotor cues to the 400 ms delay but estimated the source of the unexpected balance motion (i.e., distorted motor command – whole-body motion relationship) and broadly updated its control (Berniker and Kording, 2008; Braun et al., 2010; Krakauer and Mazzoni, 2011) to accommodate for imposed delays.
evidence: This is an inference from the generalization of learning across delays, supported by citations to theoretical frameworks.

claim: Part of the variability in whole-body sway caused by sensory manipulations is considered to represent errors in balance estimates.
source: Part of the variability in whole-body sway caused by sensory manipulations is considered to represent errors in balance estimates (Kiemel et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Imposed delays should evoke unexpected feedback errors.
source: Because imposed delays should evoke unexpected feedback errors (Blakemore et al., 1999; Farrer et al., 2008; Haering and Kiesel, 2015; Wen, 2019), the changes in vestibular-evoked muscle responses and perception with sway velocity variance may reflect that the two behavioral responses are linked to balance errors.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature on sensorimotor prediction errors.

claim: The changes in vestibular-evoked muscle responses and perception with sway velocity variance may reflect that the two behavioral responses are linked to balance errors.
source: Because imposed delays should evoke unexpected feedback errors (Blakemore et al., 1999; Farrer et al., 2008; Haering and Kiesel, 2015; Wen, 2019), the changes in vestibular-evoked muscle responses and perception with sway velocity variance may reflect that the two behavioral responses are linked to balance errors.
evidence: This is a speculation about the relationship between the measured variables.

claim: It is not explicitly clear from the data what specific component of the standing behavior can be attributed to discrepancies between actual and expected feedback.
source: However, it is not explicitly clear from our data what specific component of the standing behavior can be attributed to discrepancies between actual and expected feedback.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of a limitation in interpreting the data.

claim: Changes in standing behavior following adaptation to a delay could also be attributed to other factors induced by the imposed delays, such as a change in control policy or increased volitional control to balance.
source: Therefore, changes in standing behavior following adaptation to a delay could also be attributed to other factors induced by the imposed delays, such as a change in control policy or increased volitional control to balance (Elias et al., 2014; Ozdemir et al., 2018; Peterson and Ferris, 2019).
evidence: This is a speculation about alternative explanations, supported by citations.

claim: It is plausible that the observed changes in vestibular and perceptual responses were partially driven by whole-body motion and not solely prediction errors.
source: When accounting for this limitation, it is also plausible that the observed changes in vestibular and perceptual responses were partially driven by whole-body motion (i.e., magnitude and variability) and not solely prediction errors.
evidence: This is a speculation about alternative explanations for the findings.

claim: Vestibular responses are known to be modulated by standing kinematics.
source: For instance, vestibular responses are known to be modulated by standing kinematics (Day et al., 1997; Rasman et al., 2018; Son et al., 2008) and perceiving balance motion is related to whether the experienced motion exceeds sensory detection thresholds (Fitzpatrick and McCloskey, 1994).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Perceiving balance motion is related to whether the experienced motion exceeds sensory detection thresholds.
source: For instance, vestibular responses are known to be modulated by standing kinematics (Day et al., 1997; Rasman et al., 2018; Son et al., 2008) and perceiving balance motion is related to whether the experienced motion exceeds sensory detection thresholds (Fitzpatrick and McCloskey, 1994).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: During aging and certain diseases, the sensory and/or motor conduction times increase and may affect an individual's ability to maintain their body center of mass position within their base of support.
source: During aging and certain diseases (e.g., diabetic neuropathy or multiple sclerosis), the sensory and/or motor conduction times increase and may affect an individual's ability to maintain their body center of mass position within their base of support.
evidence: This is a general statement about clinical populations based on established knowledge.

claim: The standing balance system can be trained to accommodate a larger range of sensorimotor delays than previously predicted.
source: According to our results, the standing balance system can be trained to accommodate a larger range of sensorimotor delays than previously predicted, which may be valuable for clinical populations who are thought to experience instability and an increased risk of falls as a result of increased neural delays.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the study's findings with implications for clinical populations.

claim: Adaptation to increased neural delays with aging is thought to occur through decreased sensorimotor gains and increased ankle stiffness.
source: Adaptation to increased neural delays with aging, for example, is thought to occur through decreased sensorimotor gains and increased ankle stiffness (Le Mouel and Brette, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Training with delays may enable targeted rehabilitation of aging-related balance impairments by restoring and sustaining sensory contributions to standing balance.
source: Because our results show that training with an additional 400 ms delay can restore vestibular contributions of balance across a broad range of imposed delays (and are retained over a 3 month period), it may be possible to explore targeted rehabilitation of aging-related balance impairments by training with delays to restore and sustain sensory contributions to standing balance.
evidence: This is a speculation about potential clinical applications based on the study's findings.

claim: The manipulation altered the timing between the net output of self-generated balance motor commands and resulting sensory cues encoding whole-body and ankle motion.
source: We manipulated the delay between ankle-produced torques (measured from the force plate) and the resulting whole-body motion (angular rotation about the ankle joints). This manipulation altered the timing between the net output of self-generated balance motor commands (i.e., ankle torques) and resulting sensory cues (visual, vestibular, and somatosensory) encoding whole-body and ankle motion.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental manipulation.

claim: The timing between motor commands and part of the somatosensory signals from muscles and skin that are sensitive to muscle force or movements and pressure distribution under the feet were unaltered by the imposed delays to whole-body motion.
source: However, the timing between motor commands and part of the somatosensory signals from muscles (muscle spindles and Golgi tendon organs) and/or skin (cutaneous receptors under the feet) that are sensitive to muscle force (and related ankle torque) or movements and pressure distribution under the feet were unaltered by the imposed delays to whole-body motion.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of a limitation in the experimental manipulation.

claim: The unaltered timing of some somatosensory signals may have led to potential conflicts in the sensory coding of balance motion and may have influenced the ability to control and learn to stand with imposed delays.
source: This may have led to potential conflicts in the sensory coding of balance motion and may have influenced the ability to control and learn to stand with imposed delays.
evidence: This is a speculation about how the limitation might have affected the results.

claim: Increasing the imposed sensorimotor delays in standing balance results in unstable standing balance, attenuated vestibular control of balance, and perceptual detections of unexpected motion.
source: We observed that increasing the imposed sensorimotor delays in standing balance results in unstable standing balance, attenuated vestibular control of balance, and perceptual detections of unexpected motion.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings.

claim: The nervous system can adapt to novel sensorimotor delays and learn to maintain upright standing despite their initially disruptive influence.
source: The nervous system, however, can adapt to novel sensorimotor delays and learn to maintain upright standing despite their initially disruptive influence.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings from the training experiments.

claim: Learning to control standing balance with added sensorimotor delays is accompanied by vestibular contributions to balance partially returning and standing motion more likely to be perceived as self-generated.
source: This learning is accompanied by vestibular contributions to balance partially returning and standing motion more likely to be perceived as self-generated.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings from the vestibular and perceptual testing.

claim: The nervous system can learn to control standing balance with added sensorimotor delays by causally relating delayed whole-body sensory feedback (initially deemed unexpected) with self-generated balancing motor commands.
source: Thus, our results suggest that the nervous system can learn to control standing balance with added sensorimotor delays by causally relating delayed whole-body sensory feedback (initially deemed unexpected) with self-generated balancing motor commands.
evidence: This is the main mechanistic conclusion from the study.

claim: A total of 46 healthy adult participants participated in this study.
source: A total of 46 healthy adult participants (32 males, age: 24.0 ± 3.9 years [mean ± SD]; range 19–34 years) with no known history of neurological deficits participated in this study.
evidence: This is a description of the participant sample.

claim: The experiments were approved by the University of British Columbia Human Research Ethics Committee and conformed to the Declaration of Helsinki.
source: The experiments were approved by the University of British Columbia Human Research Ethics Committee and conformed to the Declaration of Helsinki, with the exception of registration to a database.
evidence: This is a statement about ethical approval.

claim: The robot was programmed to rotate the whole body in the AP direction about the participant's ankles.
source: The robot was programmed to rotate the whole body in the AP direction about the participant's ankles.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental setup.

claim: Angular position limits of 6° anterior and 3° posterior from vertical were imposed into the simulation to represent the physical limits of sway during standing balance.
source: Angular position limits of 6° anterior and 3° posterior from vertical were imposed into the simulation to represent the physical limits of sway during standing balance, whereby the robot constrained the angular rotation when these virtual limits were exceeded (see Materials and methods).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental setup.

claim: The delay between a position command and the measured position of the motor was estimated to be 20 ms.
source: The delay between a position command and the measured position of the motor was estimated to be 20 ms (Shepherd, 2014).
evidence: This is a technical specification of the robotic system, supported by citation.

claim: Rendering and projection of the visual scene took approximately 70 ms.
source: Rendering and projection of the visual scene took approximately 70 ms; therefore, a linear least-squares predictor algorithm was used to synchronize the visual motion (i.e., predict visual motion occurring 50 ms later) together with the motors at a delay of 20 ms (Shepherd, 2014).
evidence: This is a technical specification of the visual system, supported by citation.

claim: Thirteen healthy participants were instructed to stand quietly on a robotic balance simulator for 60 s trials while experiencing fixed imposed delays (20, 100, 200, 300, 400, 500 ms) between the torques generated at their feet and resulting whole-body motion.
source: Thirteen healthy participants were instructed to stand quietly on a robotic balance simulator for 60 s trials (Materials and methods) while experiencing fixed imposed delays (20, 100, 200, 300, 400, 500 ms) between the torques generated at their feet and resulting whole-body motion.
evidence: This is a description of the Experiment 1 protocol.

claim: Twelve participants returned ~3 months later to examine whether any learning was retained.
source: Twelve participants also returned ~3 months later to examine whether any learning was retained.
evidence: This is a description of the retention testing in Experiment 2.

claim: EVS signals with a 0–25 Hz frequency bandwidth were generated offline using custom-designed computer code.
source: EVS signals with a 0–25 Hz frequency bandwidth were generated offline using custom-designed computer code (LabVIEW 2013, National Instruments).
evidence: This is a description of the vestibular stimulation methodology.

claim: For each delay condition, EVS was delivered in four 20 s trials, resulting in a total of 80 s of data (24 total trials).
source: For each delay condition, EVS was delivered in four 20 s trials, resulting in a total of 80 s of data (24 total trials).
evidence: This is a description of the vestibular testing protocol.

claim: A total of 18 participants, 8 of which participated in the training protocol of Experiment 2, completed perceptual testing.
source: A total of 18 participants, 8 of which participated in the training protocol of Experiment 2, completed perceptual testing (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is a description of the perceptual testing participant sample.

claim: Participants balanced themselves in the robotic simulator for ~260 s in 10 separate trials during perceptual testing.
source: Participants balanced themselves in the robotic simulator for ~260 s in 10 separate trials.
evidence: This is a description of the perceptual testing protocol.

claim: In Experiment 3, participants balanced on the robotic balance system for six separate trials lasting ~260 s each.
source: Specifically, we determined (1) vestibular response attenuation in relation to when participants perceive unexpected standing behavior, and (2) the sway velocity variance associated with modulations in the vestibular and perceptual responses. Participants balanced on the robotic balance system for six separate trials lasting ~260 s each and were instructed to indicate perceived changes in balance control via button press.
evidence: This is a description of the Experiment 3 protocol.

claim: Sway velocity variance was estimated only from data in which whole-body angular position was within the virtual balance limits.
source: Sway velocity variance was estimated only from data in which whole-body angular position was within the virtual balance limits (6° anterior and 3° posterior).
